title: Breakfast at a café
goal: Order drinks and breakfast politely, count from 0 to 20, and ask how much it costs.
bekal: use *hay* to ask whether something is available

dialogs.title: Diálogo — Pidiendo el desayuno
dialogs.intro: Eight in the morning at a café in Madrid. A Spanish breakfast is short and often eaten standing at the bar.

lines.speaker: Camarero:
lines.id: Good morning. What would you like?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Quisiera un café con leche, por favor.
lines.id: I'd like a coffee with milk, please.
lines.literal: I-would-like a coffee with milk, please.

lines.speaker: Camarero:
lines.text: ¿Y para comer? Tenemos tostadas y churros.
lines.id: And to eat? We have toast and churros.
lines.literal: and for to-eat? we-have toasts and churros.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Una tostada con tomate, por favor.

lines.speaker: Camarero:
lines.id: Yes, of course. Large or small?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.id: Here you are. Thank you very much!

notes: **Quisiera is the key to politeness.** It means "I'd like", much softer than *quiero* ("I want"). In cafés, restaurants and shops, *quisiera* is almost always the right choice. And you only need this one form for now.

**Un and una.** Spanish nouns have gender: *un café* (masculine), *una tostada* (feminine). When you order, the gender decides the form of the number one — and only the number one. *Dos cafés* and *dos tostadas* use the same word.
**Por favor and gracias.** *Por favor* at the end of a request, *gracias* after you receive something. Leaving them out sounds rude to Spanish ears.

**Hay = there is / there are.** One word for singular and plural: *hay un café* (there's a café), *hay tres cafés* (there are three cafés). It never changes, and it's the most useful word for asking whether anything is available: *¿hay wifi?*, *¿hay agua?*
**¿Cuánto es? vs ¿cuánto son?** For one item, *¿cuánto es?*; when giving the total for several items, Spaniards use the plural: *son cuatro euros*. You'll hear *son* at the checkout all the time.
**Nada más** = "nothing else", the standard answer to *¿algo más?* Softer than a plain *no*.
**Aquí tiene** literally means "here you have" — said when handing something over, like "here you are". The informal version is *aquí tienes*.
**Enseguida** (sometimes written *en seguida*) = "right away". Waiters say it as they turn away; it means your order has been taken.

grammars.title: Numbers 0-20
body: The number 1 changes to match the thing being counted: *un café* but *una tostada*. The rest never change, whatever you're counting.
after: *Uno* shortens to *un* right before a masculine noun: *uno* on its own ("one!"), *un café* with a noun. The feminine form doesn't shorten: *una tostada*.
The numbers 16-19 are really *diez y seis* etc. squeezed into one word. That's why *dieciséis* has a ´ and *diecisiete* doesn't — the stress falls in a different place.

sections.title: What the waiter says, what you say

blocks.text: Café conversations almost always use exactly the same sentences. Memorize the right-hand column; just recognize the left-hand one when you hear it.

items: two pieces of toast with tomato

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with *un* or *una*.

answers: Quisiera un café con leche, por favor. — Quisiera un té sin azúcar, por favor. — Quisiera dos tostadas con tomate, por favor. — Quisiera una botella de agua sin gas, por favor. — Quisiera un zumo de naranja, por favor.
